initial_requirements: Developers building multi-agent systems need an expanded agentMom framework that provides reusable communication capabilities for agents and their conversations. Agents should be able to communicate with one recipient, selected groups, or all agents on a local network, join and leave communication groups, and choose whether messages require protection. The new framework must remain usable with applications based on the existing agentMom environment.

messages.content: What specific communication capabilities and behaviors should the expanded agentMom framework provide for agents—for example, sending to one recipient, selected groups, or all agents, joining or leaving groups, and handling protected versus unprotected messages?

At a minimum, agents should be able to send messages directly to one specific recipient, to a chosen group of agents, or broadcast to all available agents on the local network. They should also be able to join and leave groups dynamically so communication can be organized around tasks or projects. For message protection, I’d expect the sender to be able to mark a message as protected when it contains sensitive content, while unprotected messages can be handled normally; the exact protection mechanism is something we’d need to define more carefully with the technical team.

When a sender marks a message as protected, what protection mechanism should the framework use to secure it—for example, encryption, access control, or another approach—and are there any specific requirements for how protected messages should be handled end to end?

I’d expect protected messages to be secured primarily through encryption in transit, and probably also restricted so only intended recipients or authorized group members can access them. Beyond that, protected messages should stay protected end to end, meaning they shouldn’t be exposed in plain form to intermediate components, logs, or any non-authorized agent. I don’t have a fixed requirement yet on the exact algorithm or key management approach, so that would need to be confirmed with the technical team.

Do you have any preference or constraint for the encryption algorithm to be used for protected messages—for example, a specific standard, minimum strength, or requirement to align with existing agentMom or legacy-agent implementations?

We don’t have a hard mandate on a specific algorithm right now, but we would want something standard and widely accepted rather than a custom scheme. The main constraint is that it should be compatible with existing agentMom and legacy-agent setups, so if those systems already support a particular approach, we’d prefer to align with that. If there’s no existing standard in place, then I’d lean toward whatever the team considers current best practice for secure messaging.

Who are the key stakeholder roles for this expanded agentMom framework, and what core data entities or objects do they need to create, send, store, or manage (for example, agents, groups, messages, memberships, or protection settings)?

The key stakeholders are the developers who will build on the framework, the agents or applications using it, and the administrators or operators who may manage deployments and network communication behavior. The core objects we need are agents, communication groups, group memberships, messages, and some kind of protection or security setting attached to messages. We may also need conversation or delivery records for tracking, but that depends on how much history and traceability the framework is expected to keep.

Should the framework provide delivery receipts or delivery status tracking for messages, and if so, what level of confirmation or traceability do you need for direct, group, and broadcast messages, especially for protected messages?

Yes, some level of delivery status tracking would be useful, at least for direct and group messages. For direct messages, it would help to know whether the recipient got it, and for group messages a confirmation that the message was delivered to the group members or accepted for delivery would be important; for broadcast messages, a best-effort status is probably enough. For protected messages, we’d want traceability that doesn’t expose content, so the status should confirm delivery without revealing the payload.

How should the framework verify and represent agent identity and authentication for message exchange and group membership—for example, do agents need strong authenticated identities, mutual authentication, or support for anonymous/unauthenticated communication in any cases, especially when protected messages and delivery traceability are involved?

Agents should have a verified identity when they’re participating in protected messaging or joining controlled groups, because we need to know who is allowed to receive what. Mutual authentication would be preferable for trusted agent-to-agent communication, especially if delivery receipts or membership decisions are involved. I don’t think anonymous communication should be the default here; if it’s supported at all, it would need to be limited to very basic unprotected interactions and probably excluded from protected or traceable exchanges.

What should the audit logs capture for this framework—such as message events, group membership changes, delivery receipts, authentication activity, and security-related actions—and which parts of protected communication, if any, should be excluded or redacted from those logs?

The audit logs should capture the important lifecycle events like message sent, delivered, failed, group joined, group left, authentication success or failure, and any security-related changes like enabling protection or changing membership rules. For protected communication, we should log the fact that something was sent or received and who it involved, but not the message content itself or any sensitive payload details. If there are message titles, metadata, or identifiers that could reveal too much, those should be redacted or minimized as well.
